> [!NOTE]
> **New: SARIF output.** `patchledger report --format sarif` now exports the
> verified ledger for GitHub code scanning and any SARIF 2.1.0 consumer —
> with patchledger fingerprints, raw severity, and coverage honesty included.

<div align="center">

<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="./assets/banner-dark.png">
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)" srcset="./assets/banner-light.png">
  <img src="./assets/banner-dark.png" alt="PatchLedger — Security findings, verified fixed." width="100%">
</picture>

### PatchLedger is an evidence-first security finding and remediation verification platform.

-Run PatchLedger only against repositories you are authorized to assess-

It runs the scanners you already trust, unifies their findings into one
persistent, deduplicated ledger — and verifies that a vulnerability was
actually fixed, with scanner-coverage evidence, before calling it resolved.
**No proof, no "fixed."**

**This repository is PatchLedger: the full open-source CLI, run locally from
your command line.**

<p><strong>Launch PatchLedger</strong></p>

```bash
pipx install patchledger
patchledger init && patchledger scan .
```

<sub>The first scan records which of your scanners are visible — missing tools are reported, never hidden.</sub>

</div>

> [!TIP]
> **Reviewing findings with an AI assistant or a colleague?** Run
> `patchledger export-ai` — it generates a reviewer-ready prompt with the
> evidence, the questions, and explicit constraints against inventing facts.
> Fully offline; bring your own reviewer.

## What is PatchLedger?

PatchLedger is a local-first CLI that turns scattered scanner output into a
verifiable remediation ledger. It runs established security scanners against
your repository (or imports their existing reports), normalizes everything
into one consistent data model, and tracks every finding across scans — with
deterministic fingerprints, explainable risk scores, and an audit trail.

The verification step is the core: when a finding stops appearing in scans,
PatchLedger checks whether the scanners that detected it actually ran
successfully and covered the same target. Only then is the finding marked
**resolved**. Anything less is recorded as **inconclusive** — with the exact
reason attached.

<a id="why-patchledger-exists"></a>
<details>
<summary><strong>Why PatchLedger exists</strong></summary>

Teams ship code continuously but verify security fixes rarely — most pipelines
declare a finding "resolved" the moment it stops appearing in reports, even if
the scanner never ran, crashed, or didn't cover that file. False "resolved"
states are how regressions reach production unnoticed.

PatchLedger closes that gap: every scan is an immutable observation point, and
resolution claims must survive an evidence check. An honest *inconclusive*
costs one re-run; a false *fixed* costs a breach.

</details>

<a id="why-inconclusive-is-a-feature"></a>
<details>
<summary><strong>Why "inconclusive" is a feature</strong></summary>

A finding that disappears from a scan is only a <em>resolution candidate</em>.
PatchLedger verifies it against the evidence: did every scanner that ever
reported this fingerprint run successfully in the newer scan, against the same
target? Imported reports cannot assert coverage, so verifications against them
stay inconclusive by design. Scanner version changes are recorded as caveats.

Every verification decision — including the reasons and caveats — is stored in
an audit trail and rendered into reports.

</details>

## PatchLedger in action

Real output from a scan of a deliberately vulnerable fixture repository
([tests/fixtures/demo_repo](tests/fixtures/demo_repo)) — note the honest
`unavailable` row, the merged duplicates, and the explainable scores:

![PatchLedger scan and findings in the terminal](assets/terminal-demo.png)

```bash
$ patchledger verify
  FIXED VERIFIED  fp2:56e15c…  all reporting scanners ran successfully
  INCONCLUSIVE    fp2:91ac…   scanner gitleaks did not run
```

Generated example reports (JSON, Markdown, HTML) with clearly labelled
synthetic data are in [`examples/`](examples/).

## Quick start

<a id="prerequisites"></a>

### Prerequisites

- Python **3.10+**
- Any standard installer (pipx, pip, uv)
- Scanners are **optional**: install what you want, PatchLedger reports what
  is missing (see [docs/installation.md](docs/installation.md))

> [!WARNING]
> PatchLedger runs security scanners that execute code analysis against the
> target. Run it only against repositories you own or are explicitly
> authorized to assess, and sandbox scans of untrusted code — some scanners
> inherently execute project code (for example, dependency resolution can
> build sdists). See
> [Safety, scope, and limitations](#safety-scope-and-limitations).

<a id="install-and-first-scan"></a>

### Install and first scan

```bash
pipx install patchledger          # or: pip install patchledger

cd your-project
patchledger init                  # creates .patchledger/ (config + ledger db)
patchledger scan .                # runs installed scanners
patchledger findings              # the live finding ledger
patchledger history               # every recorded scan
```

<a id="verify-a-fix"></a>

### Verify a fix

```bash
# ...fix the code...

patchledger scan .                # re-scan
patchledger verify                # proof — or an honest "inconclusive"
patchledger report --format html  # self-contained report
patchledger report --format sarif # GitHub code scanning ingest
```

CI gate for any repository:

```bash
patchledger scan . --fail-on high --strict
# exit 2: findings at/above high · exit 3: incomplete scan (with --strict)
```

## Key capabilities

- **No proof, no "fixed"**: findings are only marked resolved when the
  scanners that detected them ran successfully against the same target —
  eliminating false-resolution noise from your backlog.
- **Honest scan coverage**: every scan records which tools ran, failed, or
  were missing; reports are labelled incomplete when coverage isn't full.
- **Stable fingerprints**: versioned `fp2` identity — stable across line
  shifts and formatter runs, new exactly when the flagged code changes.
- **Explainable scores**: deterministic 0–100 with every adjustment listed;
  never invents CVSS, never escalates severity on its own.
- **Scan history & diffs**: immutable scans, new/persistent/reintroduced/
  changed diffs, and a status audit trail in local SQLite.
- **Secret redaction**: credential material is redacted on ingest — before
  storage or rendering. Redaction is hygiene; rotation is the fix.
- **Offline review prompts**: `export-ai` builds a reviewer-ready prompt with
  anti-fabrication constraints, for any AI assistant or a human reviewer.
- **Local remediation knowledge**: guidance per rule family — explanation,
  consequences, fix, secure pattern — no network, no AI API.
- **Multi-format reports**: JSON, Markdown, self-contained dark HTML (no
  JavaScript), and SARIF 2.1.0 for GitHub code scanning.
- **Private by design**: runs on your machine, stores results locally, and
  makes zero network calls after installation (pip-audit's advisory-DB
  queries excepted).

## Supported scanners

| Scanner   | Adds                                  | Import formats     |
|-----------|---------------------------------------|--------------------|
| semgrep   | Broad community SAST rules            | JSON, SARIF        |
| bandit    | Python-specific issues                | JSON, SARIF        |
| pip-audit | Dependency vulnerabilities            | JSON, SARIF        |
| gitleaks  | Secrets in tree and git history       | JSON, SARIF        |
| trivy     | Filesystem vulnerabilities            | SARIF              |
| any tool  | Anything emitting SARIF 2.1.0         | SARIF              |

## Use in CI/CD

<a id="github-actions"></a>

### GitHub Actions

Copy the ready-made workflow from
[`docs/example-workflow.md`](docs/example-workflow.md) into your repository.
It runs on push and pull requests, gates on severity, and uploads reports:

```yaml
name: PatchLedger security scan

on:
  push:
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  security-scan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262 # v4

      - uses: actions/setup-python@a26af69be951a213d495a4c3e4e4022e16d87065 # v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Install PatchLedger (pinned)
        run: pip install "patchledger @ git+https://github.com/navairgap/patchledger@v0.1.1"

      - name: Run security scan
        run: |
          patchledger init
          patchledger scan . --fail-on high

      - name: Upload report artifact
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@ea165f8d65b6e75b540449e92b4886f43607fa02 # v4
        with:
          name: patchledger-report
          path: patchledger-report-*
          if-no-files-found: ignore
```

The scan exits `2` when findings meet the severity threshold (failing the
job) and `3` on incomplete scans with `--strict` — so a broken scan is never
mistaken for a clean one. PatchLedger's own CI runs the test matrix on Python
3.10–3.14 plus lint, type-check, and a wheel smoke test
([.github/workflows/ci.yml](.github/workflows/ci.yml)).

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    REPO["Repository (your code, local)"] --> RUN["Scanner runner<br/>(semgrep · gitleaks · bandit · pip-audit · trivy)"]
    RUN -->|"missing tools recorded honestly"| PARSE["Parsers<br/>(SARIF 2.1.0 · semgrep · gitleaks · bandit · pip-audit)"]
    PARSE --> NORM["Normalizer<br/>(severity maps · redaction · categories · remediation KB)"]
    NORM --> FP["Fingerprints (fp2)"]
    FP --> DEDUP["Deduplication<br/>(occurrences preserved)"]
    DEDUP --> SCORE["Scoring (explainable)"]
    SCORE --> DB[("SQLite ledger<br/>(immutable scans · audit trail)")]
    DB --> CMP["Scan comparison"]
    DB --> VER["Patch verification<br/>(coverage-aware)"]
    DB --> REP["Reports<br/>(JSON · MD · HTML · SARIF)"]
    CMP --> VER
```

Three runtime dependencies (`typer`, `pydantic`, `rich`), no server, no
telemetry, no network after installation. The full design — fingerprint
rationale, verification semantics, storage schema — is documented in
[docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md).

| [Releasing](docs/releasing.md) | Maintainer release process |

## Safety, scope, and limitations

- PatchLedger scans repositories **you are authorized to assess** and never
  transmits your code anywhere.
- It never downloads or executes scanner binaries on its own, never
  automatically modifies your files, and never suppresses findings without
  explicit configuration.
- **Scanning untrusted repositories:** PatchLedger itself does not execute
  repo scripts, but some scanners inherently do (e.g. pip-audit resolving
  dependencies can build sdists). Sandbox untrusted-target scans.
- Redaction is heuristic, not a guarantee — rotate leaked credentials.
- Findings still deserve human review: severity mapping is explicit but
  static analysis has false positives on every tool.
- Full threat model and honest limits:
  [docs/security-model.md](docs/security-model.md).

## Common questions

**Does PatchLedger need an AI API?**
No. The entire engine is deterministic and offline. `export-ai` generates a
prompt you can paste into any assistant — the tool itself never calls one.
A bring-your-own-key integration may arrive later as an optional extension.

**Does it output SARIF?**
Yes — `patchledger report --format sarif` emits SARIF 2.1.0 with
patchledger fingerprints as `partialFingerprints`, raw severity in
properties, and coverage honesty as tool notifications.

**Why didn't my disappeared finding get marked "fixed"?**
Verification requires that every scanner which ever reported the finding ran
successfully against the same target in the newer scan. Missing tools, failed
runs, and imported reports produce `inconclusive` with the reason recorded.
Re-run the missing scanner and rescan.

**Can findings from different scanners be merged?**
No — fingerprints include scanner identity on purpose. Merging semgrep and
bandit sightings would destroy the per-tool evidence that verification
depends on.

**Can I run it fully offline?**
Yes. The only outbound network use is pip-audit querying the PyPI advisory
database.

# docs/installation.md

# Installation

PatchLedger is a local CLI tool. It has no server, no telemetry, and no
network requirement after installation (except pip-audit, which queries the
PyPI advisory database).

## Requirements

- Python **3.10+** (tested through 3.14)
- pip / pipx / uv — any standard installer works

## Install PatchLedger

```bash
# Recommended: isolated CLI install
pipx install patchledger

# or into your environment
pip install patchledger

# development install from a checkout
git clone https://github.com/navairgap/patchledger
cd patchledger
pip install -e ".[dev]"
```

Once published to PyPI, the version above is the stable path. Until then,
install from a pinned git ref:

```bash
pip install "patchledger @ git+https://github.com/navairgap/patchledger@v0.1.0"
```

## Install scanners (optional, per-scanner)

PatchLedger works with whatever is installed and **reports honestly what is
missing**. Install any of these to widen coverage:

| Scanner   | Install                            | Adds                                          |
|-----------|------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| bandit    | `pip install bandit`               | Python SAST findings                          |
| pip-audit | `pip install pip-audit`            | Known vulnerabilities in Python dependencies  |
| semgrep   | `pip install semgrep`              | Broad community SAST rules                    |
| gitleaks  | system package or [release binary](https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks/releases) | Secrets in the working tree / git history |
| trivy     | system package or [release binary](https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy/releases) | Filesystem vulnerabilities via SARIF |

Check what PatchLedger can see:

```bash
patchledger doctor
```

## Initialize a project

In the repository you want to track (this creates `.patchledger/` with a
config and SQLite database):

```bash
cd your-repo
patchledger init
```

Add the ledger data to your `.gitignore` (PatchLedger suggests this but never
edits your files automatically):

```bash
echo ".patchledger/" >> .gitignore
```

## Python version support

The package targets Python 3.10+ and is tested on 3.10–3.14 in CI.

# docs/usage.md

# Usage handbook

Every PatchLedger command, every flag, and the exit codes CI relies on.

```
patchledger [--db PATH] [--debug] COMMAND
```

| Option    | Meaning                                                        |
|-----------|----------------------------------------------------------------|
| `--db`    | Path to the SQLite database (default `.patchledger/patchledger.db`) |
| `--debug` | Show full tracebacks instead of friendly error messages        |

## Commands

### `patchledger init [PATH]`

Initialize a project: creates `.patchledger/` (config + database) under PATH
(default `.`). An explicit `--db` puts the database anywhere you like.

### `patchledger scan [PATH]`

Run every enabled scanner that is installed, normalize + dedup + score the
results, and store one immutable scan.

```bash
patchledger scan .                       # default threshold from config (high)
patchledger scan . --fail-on medium      # CI gate: exit 2 on medium+ findings
patchledger scan . --strict              # exit 3 when the scan is incomplete
patchledger scan . --scanner bandit --scanner pip-audit   # override tool list
patchledger scan . --label "nightly-42"  # label the stored scan
```

After scanning, PatchLedger prints the honest tool-coverage table, the stored
finding count, and any ledger transitions (resolved / reintroduced /
inconclusive). A finding only becomes *resolved* when every scanner that ever
reported it ran successfully in the newer scan on the same target — otherwise
it is recorded as *inconclusive* (effectively still open).

### `patchledger import FILE...`

Import existing scanner reports as one scan bound to `--target` (default `.`).

```bash
patchledger import semgrep.json bandit.sarif --target .
patchledger import results.sarif --label "ci-run-123"
```

Supported formats (auto-detected from content): SARIF 2.1.0, semgrep JSON,
gitleaks JSON, bandit JSON, pip-audit JSON.

**Honesty note:** imported scans record their tools with status `imported` —
they cannot assert local scanner coverage, so resolution verification against
them is inconclusive by design.

### `patchledger findings`

Show the current per-finding ledger (open / resolved / reintroduced /
inconclusive), sorted by severity and risk score.

```bash
patchledger findings
patchledger findings --severity high          # at or above high
patchledger findings --status inconclusive    # not confirmed fixed
patchledger findings --scanner semgrep
patchledger findings --rule B602              # rule-id substring filter
patchledger findings --json                   # machine-readable
```

### `patchledger history`

List every recorded scan: id, timestamp, source (scan/import), tool statuses,
finding count.

### `patchledger compare SCAN_A SCAN_B`

Diff two scans (ids can be prefixes): new, persistent, resolved candidates,
reintroduced, changed severity, changed location. Targets that differ are
flagged as incompatible.

### `patchledger verify [--baseline ID]`

Explicitly verify resolution candidates between the previous scan and the
latest (or a chosen baseline). Prints per-fingerprint verdicts with reasons
and caveats, and persists status transitions to the audit trail.

### `patchledger report`

Generate a report for a scan (the latest by default, including a comparison
section when a previous scan exists).

```bash
patchledger report --format html --output report.html
patchledger report --format markdown
patchledger report --format json --scan 63c0fe0d
patchledger report --format sarif       # GitHub code scanning ingest
```

The HTML report is a single self-contained file: dark theme, no JavaScript,
Content-Security-Policy included, all dynamic content escaped. The SARIF
export carries normalized severity plus raw severity in properties,
patchledger fingerprints as partialFingerprints, and coverage honesty as
tool notifications.

### `patchledger export-ai`

Build a reviewer-ready prompt (Markdown by default, `--json` for structured
output) from open, reintroduced, and inconclusive findings — with explicit
constraints against inventing evidence. Works fully offline; bring your own
reviewer (human or AI).

```bash
patchledger export-ai --output review-prompt.md --max-findings 25
patchledger export-ai --min-severity high   # prioritize the review scope
```

### `patchledger doctor`

Installation health: Python version, scanner availability with versions,
config validity, database health. Missing scanners are informational, not
errors.

### `patchledger version`

Show the version.

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning                                                                 |
|------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | Success — findings may exist but are below the threshold                |
| 1    | Error — bad input, missing database, failed command                     |
| 2    | Findings at or above the `--fail-on` severity threshold (CI gate)        |
| 3    | Scan incomplete (missing/failed scanners) and `--strict` was passed      |

## Configuration

`.patchledger/config.json` (created by `init`, all keys optional):

```json
{
  "scanning":   { "enabled": ["semgrep", "gitleaks", "bandit", "pip-audit"],
                  "timeout_seconds": 600 },
  "scoring":    { "severity_base": { "critical": 90, "high": 70 },
                  "category_adjustment": { "secret": 10 } },
  "verification": { "require_coverage_asserted": true },
  "import_config": { "max_report_size_mb": 50, "disabled_rules": [] },
  "redact_secrets": true,
  "fail_on": "high"
}
```

Rule suppression requires an explicit `disabled_rules` entry — PatchLedger
never hides findings silently, and every suppression is counted and reported
on import/scan.

# docs/architecture.md

# Architecture

This document explains how PatchLedger is built, why the pieces are shaped
the way they are, and where the documented limits live.

## The pipeline

```
Repository (your code, local)
      |
      v
Scanner runner  ─── semgrep / gitleaks / bandit / pip-audit / trivy
      |               (as installed; missing tools recorded honestly)
      v
Parsers ─────── SARIF 2.1.0 · semgrep JSON · gitleaks JSON · bandit JSON
      |         pip-audit JSON   (format auto-detected from content)
      v
Normalizer ──── severity maps · secret redaction · categories · remediation KB
      |
      v
Fingerprints (fp2) ──► Deduplication ──► Risk scoring
      |
      v
SQLite ledger ──── scans (immutable) · findings · occurrences · status_history
      |
      +──────────────┬───────────────────┐
      v              v                   v
Scan comparison  Patch verification  Reports (JSON / MD / HTML)
      |              |                   |
      └──────────────┴───────────────────┘
                     v
               CLI (Typer + Rich) · GitHub Actions integration
```

Source layout: `src/patchledger/` with one module per stage (mirrors the
diagram); tests under `tests/` with real scanner reports recorded as fixtures.

## Data model

* **`Finding`** — the normalized unit: fingerprint, scanner, rule, severity,
  confidence, category, title, description, location, evidence, remediation,
  score + score factors, status, and occurrences.
* **`Occurrence`** — one scanner's sighting. Deduplication merges findings
  that share a fingerprint but never discards occurrences; each keeps its own
  evidence and metadata (scanner metadata is preserved verbatim, never
  interpreted).
* **`Scan`** — one immutable observation point: target path, git commit/branch
  when available, source (`scan` or `import`), and per-tool statuses
  (`ran / failed / unavailable / skipped / imported`).
* **`status_history`** — an explicit audit trail of ledger transitions
  (resolved / inconclusive / reintroduced) with reasons and verification
  evidence as JSON.

## Storage

SQLite (WAL mode, foreign keys ON) at `.patchledger/patchledger.db`.
Schema versioning lives in `schema_meta.schema_version` with sequential
migrations in `storage.py`. Multi-row inserts are transactional: a crash
cannot leave a half-written scan. Scans carry a monotonic `seq` so
"latest scan" is deterministic even when two scans land in the same
clock second.

## Fingerprints (`fp2`)

```
fingerprint = "fp2:" + sha256(fp_version, scanner, rule_id, path, message, evidence)[:32hex]
```

* **Message + evidence, not line numbers.** The message carries rule
  semantics; the snippet distinguishes findings whose messages are generic
  (bandit's `B101` on several assert lines). Line numbers are excluded so
  edits above the finding don't change identity, while edits *to* the flagged
  line legitimately produce a new identity.
* **Scanner identity, not file format.** Importing semgrep output twice in
  different formats is stable *within* a format. Documented limit: formats
  that differ in whether they carry snippets produce different fingerprints
  (`tests/test_normalizer.py` demonstrates this). The primary pipeline always
  uses one consistent format per tool, so cross-scan fingerprints are stable.
* **Versioned.** The `fp2:` prefix lets future identity changes coexist with
  history.

## Verification semantics

The differentiator. A finding absent from the newer scan is a *resolution
candidate*. It becomes `resolved` only when **all** of:

1. Every scanner that ever reported the fingerprint appears in the current
   scan with status `ran` (a real local run).
2. The current scan targeted the same path as the last observation.
3. The current scan is not an imported report (imports cannot assert
   coverage).

Otherwise the state is `inconclusive` — explicitly *not* fixed — with the
reasons recorded. Scanner version changes between baseline and current are
recorded as caveats (rule sets may differ) without blocking verification.
All of these behaviors are pinned by `tests/test_verification.py`.

## Risk scoring

Deterministic and fully explained: a base score per normalized severity plus
documented adjustments for scanner confidence, evidence presence, and
category (secrets and injections weigh more). Every adjustment is listed on
the finding. PatchLedger never invents CVSS scores or escalates severity on
its own. Rules are configurable in `.patchledger/config.json`.

## Security posture of PatchLedger itself

See `docs/security-model.md` for the threat model. Headlines: argv-list
subprocess execution only (never a shell, never auto-downloaded tools),
parameterized SQL everywhere, strict size-capped JSON parsing, HTML reports
with zero JavaScript and a restrictive CSP, secret redaction on ingest, and
no network access after installation (except pip-audit's advisory DB).

# docs/security-model.md

# Security model

PatchLedger is a security tool, so it is held to the standard it enforces.
This document states the threat model, the guarantees, and the honest limits.

## What PatchLedger is for

Scanning and verifying **repositories you are authorized to assess**. It is
a local CLI: source code, findings, and reports stay on your machine unless
you choose to publish them (e.g. upload a CI artifact).

## Guarantees

### Process execution
* Scanners run through `subprocess.run` with **argv lists** — never
  `shell=True`, never string interpolation into a command line.
* The executable is the one `shutil.which`/config resolved; argv[0] is pinned
  to the discovered path (no PATH re-resolution at exec time).
* Hard timeouts kill runaway scanners; stdout/stderr are captured, bounded,
  and only excerpted into notes on failure.
* PatchLedger **never downloads or executes** tools on its own. `doctor`
  reports availability; you install scanners yourself.

### Input handling
* Report files are size-capped (default 50 MB, hard absolute cap 512 MB),
  parsed strictly (`NaN`/`Infinity` rejected), with actionable errors for
  malformed input and clear behavior for adversarial nesting.
* Parser code treats report content as data only — no `eval`, no dynamic
  imports, no templated execution. SARIF URIs are URL-decoded and
  path-normalized, never executed or resolved into command lines.

### Storage
* Every SQL statement is parameterized; there is no string-built SQL.
* WAL mode + foreign keys ON; transactions wrap scan inserts so crashes
  cannot corrupt state.

### Secrets
* gitleaks material is redacted on ingest: raw `Secret`/`Match` values never
  reach storage; evidence carries prefix/suffix/length only.
* Secret-category evidence from any scanner has quoted literals, PEM blocks,
  and common token formats (AWS/GitHub/Slack/Stripe/GitLab) redacted.
* Redaction is best-effort and documented as such — **rotation is the real
  fix**; removing a value from reports does not un-leak anything.
* PatchLedger has no telemetry, no network calls at runtime (except
  pip-audit's advisory DB queries), and never transmits your code anywhere.

### Reports
* The HTML report contains **zero JavaScript** and ships a
  `Content-Security-Policy` of `default-src 'none'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'`
  — the script-injection sink does not exist. Every dynamic value passes
  through `html.escape`; hostile-payload tests pin this.
* Markdown reports escape table pipes so findings cannot break out of their
  structure.
* Example reports are clearly labelled **SYNTHETIC EXAMPLE DATA** and are
  generated from fabricated findings — never presented as real scans.

### Verification honesty
* A finding is `resolved` only with full scanner coverage (see
  `docs/architecture.md`). Missing tools, failed runs, different targets, and
  imported reports all yield **inconclusive** — never a silent "fixed".
* Incomplete scans are labelled as such in every report and in the CLI.

## Honest limits

* **Coverage is approximated per tool run**, not per file: if semgrep ran
  successfully on the target, its rules are considered to have covered the
  tree. Tools' internal ignore files (`.semgrepignore`, `.gitignore` for
  gitleaks) are not currently parsed; a rule that never sees a file can still
  allow a false-verified resolution in that corner.
* **Fingerprints are content-based.** Two byte-identical flagged snippets for
  the same rule at the same path merge (identical issues are the same issue).
* **Cross-format imports** of the same tool can produce different
  fingerprints when one format carries snippets the other doesn't.
* **Redaction is heuristic.** Novel secret formats may pass through in
  evidence; treat all PatchLedger output as containing the secrets your code
  contains until proven otherwise.
* **Risk scores are prioritization aids**, not measurements; they are
  deterministic and explainable but not a substitute for human triage.
* **Severity ceiling for coarse sources.** SARIF and semgrep only expose
  error/warning/note levels, which normalize to at most `high`. Sources that
  report `critical` explicitly can trigger a critical; `--fail-on critical`
  therefore prints an explanatory notice and cannot rely on coarse sources
  to ever produce critical findings.
* **Scanning untrusted repositories.** PatchLedger never executes repo
  scripts itself, but some *scanners* do inherently: `pip-audit -r
  requirements.txt` performs dependency resolution that can build sdists
  (executing `setup.py`), and tools may auto-load repo-level configs
  (e.g. `gitleaks.toml`) that change their behavior. When scanning code you
  do not trust, run PatchLedger inside a sandbox (container, throwaway VM)
  — that is the standard practice for running arbitrary scanners against
  untrusted trees, and it applies here too. Configuration under
  `.patchledger/` controls thresholds and rule suppression, **never tool
  execution**: there is deliberately no config-driven tool search path.
* **Markdown reports** escape structure-forging metacharacters and size
  evidence fences dynamically, but Markdown is a simpler format than the
  zero-JavaScript HTML report; prefer HTML when sharing reports.

## Dependencies

Runtime dependencies are deliberately minimal (`typer`, `pydantic`, `rich`)
and CI runs `pip-audit` on the project itself. Dependency advisories that
affect PatchLedger are treated as security bugs — see `SECURITY.md`.

# docs/faq.md

# FAQ

## Does PatchLedger need an AI API?

No. The core engine — scanning, normalization, deduplication, scoring,
comparison, verification, reporting — is fully deterministic and works
offline. `patchledger export-ai` generates a structured review prompt you can
paste into *any* external assistant or hand to a human reviewer; the prompt
carries the evidence and forbids inventing more. A bring-your-own-key AI
integration may arrive later as an optional extension — it will never be
required.

## Where does my code go?

Nowhere. Scanning runs locally against your working tree. The only outbound
network use is pip-audit querying the PyPI advisory database. Reports are
written where you point them (and uploaded as CI artifacts only if you
configure that).

## A scanner disappeared between scans — is that finding "fixed"?

No — it is *inconclusive*. PatchLedger only marks a finding resolved when
every scanner that ever reported it ran successfully in the newer scan on the
same target. Missing tools, failed scans, and imported reports all produce
inconclusive verdicts with recorded reasons. Run the missing scanner and
rescan to turn inconclusive into verified.

## Why did my finding's fingerprint change after I edited the flagged line?

By design: the fingerprint includes the code snippet, and the snippet changed.
The old finding becomes a resolution candidate (verified fixed if coverage
was sufficient) and the edited line appears as a new finding. Edits elsewhere
in the file do *not* change the fingerprint.

## Can two different scanners' findings be merged?

No. Fingerprints include the scanner identity, so semgrep and bandit sightings
of the same problem stay separate findings — merging them would lose the
per-tool evidence that patch verification depends on.

## How do I silence a rule?

Only via explicit configuration: put the rule id in
`.patchledger/config.json` under `import_config.disabled_rules`. Suppression
is never silent — the scan/import output reports exactly what was suppressed
and how often.

## Are example reports real scan data?

No. Everything under `examples/` and the website's report preview is
synthetic, clearly labelled, and generated by `scripts/generate_examples.py`
from fabricated findings.

## Is the HTML report safe to share?

It is a single self-contained file with no JavaScript and a restrictive CSP;
all dynamic content is escaped. It does contain your findings — including
redacted evidence — so treat it as sensitive and share it deliberately.

## Does it run on Windows/macOS?

The package targets any OS with Python 3.10+ (console scripts, no compiled
deps). Most testing happens on Linux; scanner availability varies per OS the
same way it would for the scanners themselves. Windows-specific issues are
welcome bug reports.

## How is this different from just running the scanners?

Running the scanners gives you five report formats, five severity scales, no
history, and no proof. PatchLedger gives you one ledger with stable identity
across time, explainable scores, and — the point — verification that a fix
actually happened before anyone marks it done.

# docs/example-workflow.md

# Example: run PatchLedger in your repository's CI

Copy this file into your repository as
`.github/workflows/patchledger-scan.yml`. It installs PatchLedger, scans the
repository on every push and pull request, uploads the HTML report as a
workflow artifact, and fails the job when findings meet or exceed the
severity threshold.

Notes:

* `--fail-on high` means: exit code 2 when any open/reintroduced finding is
  high or critical. Adjust to `medium`, `critical`, or `low`.
* Scanner availability is honest: if a scanner is not installed, PatchLedger
  reports it as unavailable instead of claiming a complete scan. Install the
  tools you want (see docs/installation.md) to widen coverage.
* The PatchLedger database lives in `.patchledger/` inside the runner
  workspace — it is ephemeral per CI run, which is fine for threshold gates.
  Durable scan history and patch verification work best from local runs.
* Once PatchLedger is published to PyPI you can replace the pip install line
  with `pip install patchledger`.

```yaml
name: PatchLedger security scan

on:
  push:
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  security-scan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262 # v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0  # full history helps gitleaks if it is installed

      - uses: actions/setup-python@a26af69be951a213d495a4c3e4e4022e16d87065 # v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Install PatchLedger (pinned)
        run: pip install "patchledger @ git+https://github.com/navairgap/patchledger@v0.1.0"

      - name: Run security scan
        run: |
          patchledger init
          patchledger scan . --fail-on high

      - name: Upload report artifact
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@ea165f8d65b6e75b540449e92b4886f43607fa02 # v4
        with:
          name: patchledger-report
          path: |
            patchledger-report-*.html
            patchledger-report-*.json
          if-no-files-found: ignore
```

## Customizing

* **Different threshold:** change `--fail-on` (severity: `critical`, `high`,
  `medium`, `low`). Exit code 2 fails the job; a clean scan exits 0.
* **Fail on incomplete scans:** add `--strict` to the scan step — the job
  then also fails (exit 3) when scanners were unavailable or failed.
* **Specific scanners only:** pass `--scanner bandit --scanner pip-audit`
  (repeatable flag) to override the configured scanner list.
* **Configuration file:** commit a `.patchledger/config.json` to your
  repository (created by `patchledger init`) to control scoring rules,
  disabled rules, and the default threshold. Rule suppression always
  requires this explicit file — PatchLedger never hides findings silently.

# docs/releasing.md

# Releasing PatchLedger (maintainer guide)

## Checklist before tagging

1. `pytest`, `ruff check src tests scripts`, `mypy` — all green.
2. Update `CHANGELOG.md`: move the unreleased section to the new version and
   date; add any last entries.
3. Bump `version` in `pyproject.toml` (and `src/patchledger/__init__.py`),
   commit.
4. `uv build` and smoke-test in a fresh venv:

   ```bash
   uv venv /tmp/pl-check
   uv pip install --python /tmp/pl-check/bin/python dist/*.whl
   /tmp/pl-check/bin/patchledger version
   /tmp/pl-check/bin/patchledger doctor
   ```

## Tag and publish

```bash
git tag -a vX.Y.Z -m "PatchLedger vX.Y.Z"
git push origin vX.Y.Z
```

The `Release` workflow builds the distribution, smoke-tests the wheel, and
publishes a GitHub Release with generated notes plus both artifacts.

## PyPI (when enabled)

Publishing to PyPI is intentionally not automated until the project is
officially on PyPI. When it is: add an `pypi publish` job using trusted
publishing (PyPI OIDC, no API tokens) that uploads `dist/*` after the smoke
test, and switch the user-facing example workflow from the pinned git
install to `pip install patchledger`.

## After release

- Verify the GitHub Release page renders notes and assets.
- Update the website roadmap section if the release changed status claims.
- Announce with a link to the changelog, not to a marketing claim.
